report:
## Conclusion

The claim that "capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans" is **not supported by current evidence**. Capsaicin shows anticancer effects only in laboratory (in vitro) and animal studies — there are no clinical trials demonstrating it treats breast cancer tumors in people.

## What the evidence actually shows

**Lab studies are promising but not human treatment data.** Multiple in vitro studies show capsaicin inhibits proliferation and induces apoptosis in breast cancer cell lines (e.g., MDA-MB-231, MCF-7) by suppressing proteins like FBI-1 and altering signaling pathways (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33173974/, https://www.dovepress.com/capsaicin-inhibits-proliferation-and-induces-apoptosis-in-breast-cance-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DDDT). These are cells in a dish, not humans.

**Human clinical trials involving capsaicin and breast cancer exist, but for pain, not treatment.** The CAPTRANE and QUCIP trials tested capsaicin patches for managing chemotherapy-induced neuropathic pain in breast cancer patients — not for shrinking tumors or curing cancer (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11763653/).

**Experts explicitly caution against overstating the claim.** A comprehensive review states "the clinical value of per os capsaicin to complement chemotherapy is still speculative," and notes delivery challenges — capsaicin from food or inhalation is "insufficient" to reach tumors therapeutically (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/). Snopes' fact-check similarly concludes that while capsaicin has cancer-fighting properties in the lab, "its use as an anti-cancer therapy in humans is far from certain" (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/).

Additionally, some literature raises safety concerns that capsaicin's effects on cancer are inconsistent — it may act as either a promoter or preventive depending on context, adding further uncertainty.

**Bottom line:** Capsaicin is an interesting research subject for cancer biology, and existing human trials use it for symptom relief, but it is not an established or clinically proven treatment for breast cancer.
